issues.explanation: 'Noticing Weapons' is a poor fit for the stated trauma of physical abuse by a romantic partner unless there is evidence of weapon-related assault or generalized violence cues; the rest of the profile centers on interpersonal abuse and nonspecific danger rather than weapon-focused threat monitoring, so this item is hard to reconcile with the trauma context.

'Inaction Guilt' is clinically questionable in this context because it implies self-blame for not doing more to stop the abuse, which is less coherent with an ongoing coercive partner-abuse formulation than appraisals centered on shame, powerlessness, betrayal, or worthlessness. It is not impossible, but paired with the rest of the profile it stands out as weakly aligned with the trauma narrative and node pattern.

vignette: Rajiv had always been meticulous about his work as a tax inspector. He took pride in ensuring every detail was accounted for, every discrepancy resolved. But it wasn't just numbers that had to add up; Rajiv's life had to be controlled, predictable. Ever since the abuse he suffered at the hands of his ex-partner, Pratap, three years ago, Rajiv felt like he was walking on eggshells. The memories of those violent episodes still lingered, fragmented and disquieting. Sudden pieces would surface without warning - a sound, a smell, a certain tone of voice - and transport him back to that dark time. He recalled the night Pratap slammed his head against the wall, threatening to "make him pay" for questioning his spending habits. But there were also gaps in his memory, parts he couldn't quite grasp no matter how hard he tried. Like what happened after he blacked out from the blows. These lacunae only fueled Rajiv's anxiety. Pratap had been charming at first, showering Rajiv with affection and attention. But soon, his words turned to venom, chipping away at Rajiv's self-worth. "You're nothing without me," Pratap would say. Rajiv began to feel like an object, not a person - dehumanized, stripped of agency. Even now, as he navigated the crowded streets or met with clients, he felt trapped, his back against a wall where he could see everyone and everything. Lately, exhaustion had become Rajiv's constant companion. He'd wake up in the dead of night, his heart racing, after Pratap invaded his dreams once more. It was as if his body was perpetually on high alert, bracing for impact. Simple tasks like grocery shopping or meeting with friends left him drained. His wife, Meena, noticed the change too; she'd comment on how tired he looked, but Rajiv couldn't explain it to her - not without reliving the memories. Unpredictability terrified Rajiv. He avoided spontaneous outings, fearing that a sudden confrontation or unexpected noise would send him spiraling back into the past. In meetings with clients, he found himself scanning the room for potential threats, his mind racing through worst-case scenarios. Even walking home from work became an ordeal; he'd constantly check behind him, convinced someone was lurking in the shadows. These days, Rajiv's mantra had become "nothing good can happen to me anymore." It was a feeling of hopelessness that seeped into every aspect of his life. Meena tried to reassure him, but even her words felt hollow. He knew he needed help; the weight of these memories and fears was crushing him. Yet, seeking therapy made Rajiv anxious - what if it brought up more than he could handle? The night before their intake session, Rajiv lay awake, his mind racing with all the things that could go wrong. What if the therapist didn't understand? What if they pushed him too hard? As the sun began to rise, Meena gently coaxed him out of bed, urging him to take this first step towards healing. For Rajiv, it was a tentative beginning - but one he knew he couldn't avoid any longer.
